title: Named as an executor: first decisions in the UK
dek: Check the national estate process, your options about acting, and the duties that come before distributions, with records for questions and decisions.
metaDescription: Check the national estate process, your options about acting, and the duties that come before distributions, with records for questions and decisions.

paragraphs: If you are named executor in a UK will, first identify the applicable national estate process, decide whether you can act and preserve the information needed to administer the estate. Do not assume one UK-wide form or that finding your name lets you complete every transaction. Probate in England and Wales, Scottish confirmation and Northern Ireland procedures differ.

You may have agreed years earlier without seeing the eventual property, debts or family situation. Before promising beneficiaries a payment date, establish what must be done and whether you need professional help. This is general administration guidance, not legal advice or a complete procedure for every UK estate.

body.heading: Before substantive administration
items: Find the original will and amendments, identify every named executor and check any substitute appointment. Preserve documents rather than annotating or dividing them.
Establish the relevant jurisdiction and ask about cross-border property or domicile uncertainty. Do not select a court only because it is nearest to you.
List urgent care, security, insurance and business issues. Ask who may handle them while authority and grant requirements are being established.
If you do not want to act, get advice about your options before taking substantive steps. Disclose anything already done; do not guess whether it counts as administration.
Create an initial asset, ownership and liability list. Note unknowns instead of assuming every pension, policy and joint account falls into the distributable estate.
Keep correspondence, expenses and decisions dated. Do not mix funds or promise an inheritance before claims, tax and authority questions are understood.

body.heading: Use the correct official route
rows: GOV.UK applying for probate and estate-administration guidance.
That every estate needs a grant, or that renunciation and power reserved are the same.
Scottish Courts guidance on dealing with a deceased estate and confirmation.
That England/Wales probate forms or inheritance rules apply.
NI Direct probate guidance and its own application process.
That the England/Wales procedure for reserving power transfers unchanged.

body.heading: Deciding not to act needs the right procedure
paragraphs: For England and Wales, [GOV.UK explains options where there is a will](https://www.gov.uk/applying-for-probate/if-theres-a-will). Where more than one executor is named, power reserved can retain the ability to apply later; renunciation gives up the right to apply through its stated process. These are different decisions with different effects. Check the current form and conditions rather than copying a letter found online.

[NI Direct](https://www.nidirect.gov.uk/articles/probate) describes its own reserved-power and renunciation position. In Scotland, ask a Scottish solicitor or the relevant court about your circumstances rather than using an England/Wales form. If you have already started dealing with the estate or a grant has issued, get advice before assuming you can simply withdraw.

Helping with immediate funeral or safety arrangements is not a reason to make your own legal judgment about whether you have committed to the full role. Describe the exact acts to an adviser. If another executor will act, agree who will preserve records and communicate while the formal position is settled.

body.heading: Invented example: two executors with different capacity
paragraphs: A will names two siblings. One can manage paperwork now; the other is caring for a child and cannot take on routine administration. They identify the England/Wales route and ask about applying with power reserved to the second executor rather than describing both siblings as having renounced.

Before choosing, they check whether either has already taken substantive steps and what notices or written communication are needed. If the same family were dealing with a Scottish estate, they would not copy this option automatically. The example demonstrates a question to ask, not a recommendation for every joint appointment.

body.heading: The role lasts beyond obtaining a grant
paragraphs: [GOV.UK's estate overview](https://www.gov.uk/probate-estate) describes responsibility for estate assets during administration. The work can include identifying property, establishing values and ownership, collecting assets through the appropriate process, dealing with liabilities and tax, then distributing and accounting. Obtaining a grant is a milestone, not proof the estate is ready to pay out.

[Scottish Courts' confirmation guide](https://www.scotcourts.gov.uk/taking-action/dealing-with-a-deceaseds-estate-in-scotland/guide-to-dealing-with-a-deceaseds-estate-in-scotland/) explains the estate inventory in its own system. Do not reuse an informal family estimate where the process requires a supported value. Seek suitable valuation or tax advice for property, a business or uncertain ownership.

body.heading: Separate debts, tax and beneficiaries' expectations
paragraphs: Record known bills, possible claims and the tax questions requiring professional review. Do not pay creditors simply in order of arrival or distribute the apparent bank balance without reserves and the required checks. If the estate may be insolvent, stop and ask about the applicable priority rules. A friendly family agreement cannot necessarily remove another claimant's rights.

The deceased person's final tax position and income arising during administration can be different issues. Ask which information HMRC and the relevant estate process require for the date of death and estate circumstances. This guide deliberately does not supply a universal tax threshold, clearance period or deadline.

Ask a solicitor about creditor notices and any applicable protective process before relying on them. Such notices are not a universal UK immunity from every claim. Disputed entitlement, dependants' claims, foreign assets, missing funds, capacity concerns or plans for an executor to buy estate property need particular care.

body.heading: Ask before taking the next step

items.line: I am named executor, the estate appears to involve [assets and debts], and these actions have already happened: [facts]. Which national process applies, can I step aside, and what must be protected now?
I am confirming authority, ownership and the estate's liabilities. I cannot promise a distribution date yet. I will update you when [specific information] is confirmed.

body.heading: Agree help, costs and a manageable record
paragraphs: If using a professional, ask who is the client, what work is included, how fees are calculated, who authorizes extra work and what you remain responsible for. Do not assume every proposed expense can be reimbursed from the estate without question. Keep the engagement and supporting invoices.

Record the date, transaction, amount, evidence and reason for every estate payment or receipt. Keep an issues list with an owner and next action rather than relying on messages between relatives. Beneficiaries need accurate progress information, but a fixed completion promise is unreliable where sales, tax, claims or disputes control the timetable.

For registration and immediate notifications, use [the UK first-steps guide](/guides/what-to-do-when-a-parent-dies-uk). For this decision, the main outcome is simpler: you know the jurisdiction, your intended role, the evidence of authority needed and which action cannot safely wait.

items.q: Does agreeing during their lifetime mean I must act?
items.a: Not necessarily, but you should establish the correct national procedure and disclose what you have already done. Options and consequences differ between declining before acting and leaving after substantive administration or a grant. Get advice before signing a renunciation or assuming silence transfers the role to someone else.

items.q: Is power reserved the same as renunciation?
items.a: No. In England and Wales, power reserved can preserve the right to apply later where other executors are applying, while renunciation gives up that right through the stated process. Northern Ireland has its own position and Scotland uses a different system. Verify the applicable route before choosing forms.

items.q: Can I pay beneficiaries once probate is granted?
items.a: A grant does not itself resolve debts, tax, disputed ownership or other claims. Check the estate's liabilities, required procedures and reserves before distributing. If there is uncertainty or pressure to pay early, seek advice and explain which issue is outstanding rather than treating the grant date as an automatic payout deadline.
